title: Booze had role in cop shooting ; Man was drunk, inquest told
article: Byron Debassige's blood-alcohol level was three times over the limit to drive when he came at two cops with a knife before being shot four times and killed in 2008, a coroner's inquest heard Monday.
"He would have had at least 10 drinks," said Marie Elliot, the toxicologist who did tests on Debassige's body, adding that she also found THC in his system.
"You would have seen signs of alcohol use such as disorientation. Alcohol has an effect on judgment and there is a decreased perception of risk," she testified.

In February 2008, Debassige stole two lemons from a store at Yonge St. and Davisville Ave. and was confronted by staff. He pulled a knife, which led to an altercation with police in a park by Davisville subway station.
The inquest heard that the 28-year-old had a troubled youth and struggled with substance abuse problems. He had also been diagnosed as a schizophrenic.
Debassige, who was pronounced dead at St. Michael's Hospital, suffered three categories of injuries, Dr. John Doucet, the pathologist who performed the autopsy, told the inquest.
"He had a number of gunshot wounds to his chest and stomach, minor blunt-force injuries and injuries on his wrists due to the handcuffs," Doucet said.
"The shots went through several vital organs, causing extensive internal bleeding. Three of the shots on their own could have been lethal."
Joseph Markson, lawyer for the two police officers, said Debassige's death is sad and tragic.

"When someone is coming at you with a knife, you must live or die in that moment. How could it have been known he had a history of mental illness? His tragic decision put the officers' lives in danger and they are trained to shoot to stop the threat," Markson said.
Police have a lack of understanding when it comes to mental illness, said Barry Swadron, lawyer for the Debassige family.

"Our concern is the police will keep doing the same thing and mentally ill people with knives get shot dead. If police approached Byron calmly there would have been a better outcome. He would have been allowed to live," Swadron said.
